newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fed's Greenspan urges fast Japan financial reform.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Greenspan urges fast Japan financial reform.

text.p: Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan Monday urged Japan to quickly implement its planned "Big Bang" financial reforms while tackling its banking system's bad loan woes at the same time.
Greenspan, in Tokyo for two days of meetings with Japanese financial and monetary officials, made the plea in talks with Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka, a ministry official told reporters.

Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week unveiled a five-year "Big Bang" plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets by 2001 in order to catch up with reforms carried out more than a decade ago in Europe and North America.
Greenspan welcomed the plans and urged Mitsuzuka to speed up the process, the ministry official said.

He also said U.S. securities houses, which went through the same process of brokerage commission liberalisation in 1975, had worried at the time that liberalisation of commission fees would affect their profits. But trading volume increased and the liberalisation proved a success, he was quoted as saying.
The two men also discussed currencies, but the official declined to elaborate.

Greenspan, who as Fed chairman heads the U.S. central banking system, welcomed Japan's efforts to increase the independence of its central bank and make the Bank of Japan's decision-making on monetary policy more transparent.

Last week, advisers to the prime minister proposed giving the Bank of Japan more say in forming monetary policy, but stopped short of suggesting it be given the independence which its foreign peers enjoy.
The advisory panel proposed curbing some of the government's authority over the central bank, but also said the Bank of Japan should disclose more about its operations.
The ministry official also quoted Greenspan as saying that the European Union's move towards economic union would create a larger economic power than Japan or the United States.

Mitsuzuka, meanwhile, told Greenspan that Japanese financial firms were steadily dealing with their bad loan problems and that Tokyo's financial system was capable of handling the situation, the official said.
Greenspan said Japan needed to tackle financial reform and the bad loan issue simultaneously to improve its financial system effectively, the official added.
Japan's banking system has been struggling with the legacy of bad loans inherited when its late 1980s "bubble economy" of sky-high land and share prices burst.
Most big banks are past the worst of the problem, but smaller institutions still face difficulties.
